content.text: What Is an Algorithm?

Topic 3.3 is where we begin building algorithms. Before diving into arithmetic, it is essential to understand what an algorithm is, how it can be expressed, and what the fundamental building blocks of every algorithm are. These concepts underlie everything in Unit 3.

content.definition: A finite set of instructions that accomplishes a specific task. Every algorithm can be constructed using combinations of sequencing, selection, and iteration.

content.text: The word 'finite' is important — an algorithm must have a definite end. An infinite loop is not an algorithm because it never finishes. Every algorithm has a beginning, a sequence of steps, and an end.

content.definition: Algorithms can be expressed in natural language, diagrams, pseudocode, and visual or textual programming languages. Algorithms executed by programs are implemented using programming languages.

rows: Written in plain human language as steps
Step 1: Add all numbers. Step 2: Divide the sum by the count. Step 3: Return the result.
Visual representation of steps and decisions
Boxes and arrows showing the flow from start to sum to divide to end
Structured code-like language not tied to any specific language
sum ← 0; FOR EACH n IN list { sum ← sum + n }; RETURN sum / LENGTH(list)
Actual code in a real language like Python, Java, or AP CSP pseudocode
Implemented as executable code on a computer

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: The same algorithm can be expressed in many different ways — natural language, a diagram, pseudocode, or code — and it is still the same algorithm. The representation changes but the instructions and the result do not. On the AP exam you may be asked to trace pseudocode, read a diagram, or understand a natural language description — they all describe algorithms.
The Three Building Blocks of Every Algorithm

content.term: Three Building Blocks of Every Algorithm
content.definition:
Every algorithm can be constructed using combinations of:
1. Sequencing — executing steps in order
2. Selection — choosing which steps to execute based on a condition
3. Iteration — repeating steps
The application of each step of an algorithm in the order in which the code statements are given. Sequential statements execute in the order they appear in the code segment.

rows: Executes each step in the order given — top to bottom
x ← 5 then y ← x + 3 then DISPLAY y
Chooses which steps execute based on a condition
REPEAT n TIMES and REPEAT UNTIL loops

content.text: This is one of the most fundamental facts in all of computing: every algorithm that has ever been written or ever will be written can be expressed using only these three building blocks. You do not need any other structures. Sequencing, selection, and iteration together are computationally complete.
Code Statements and Clarity

content.definition: A part of program code that expresses an action to be carried out. Clarity and readability are important considerations when expressing an algorithm in a programming language.

content.text: Clarity and readability are not just stylistic preferences — they are explicitly identified in the CED as important considerations when expressing an algorithm in a programming language. A correct algorithm that no one can read or maintain is less useful than one that is both correct and clear. This is why meaningful variable names, good structure, and comments matter.
Expressions

content.definition: Can consist of a value, a variable, an operator, or a procedure call that returns a value. Expressions are evaluated to produce a single value following a set order of operations defined by the programming language.

content.text: An expression is anything that evaluates to a single value. This includes simple values like 5, variables like x, operations like x + 3, or procedure calls like LENGTH(aList). No matter how complex the expression, it always reduces to one single value when evaluated.

rows: A random integer from 1 to the list's length

content.text: Arithmetic Operators

content.definition: Include addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), division (/), and modulus (MOD). The MOD operator returns the remainder when a is divided by b. Example: 17 MOD 5 = 2. MOD has the same precedence as * and /.

rows: Produces exact decimal — NOT integer division

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Division in AP CSP produces the EXACT decimal result — not truncated integer division. 17 / 5 = 3.4, not 3. This is different from many real programming languages where integer division truncates. Always compute the full decimal answer.
The MOD Operator in Depth

The MOD operator is one of the most tested operators on the AP exam. a MOD b returns the remainder when a is divided by b. In AP CSP, a must be an integer ≥ 0 and b must be an integer > 0. MOD has the same precedence as * and / — it is evaluated before + and -, and left to right when alongside * or /.

content.code:
-- How MOD works: a MOD b = remainder when a is divided by b
17 MOD 5 = 2    -- 17 = 3×5 + 2 → remainder is 2
20 MOD 4 = 0    -- 20 = 5×4 + 0 → no remainder (evenly divisible)
7  MOD 2 = 1    -- 7 = 3×2 + 1  → remainder is 1
10 MOD 3 = 1    -- 10 = 3×3 + 1 → remainder is 1
1  MOD 5 = 1    -- 1 = 0×5 + 1  → remainder is 1 (a < b, so result = a)

rows: Check if a number is even
Even numbers have no remainder when divided by 2
Check if a number is odd
Odd numbers have remainder 1 when divided by 2
True when number divides evenly into n with no remainder
The units digit is always the remainder when divided by 10
Check if a is less than b
a MOD b = a (when a < b)
When a is smaller than b, the remainder is just a

content.text: Order of Operations

The order of operations used in mathematics applies when evaluating expressions in AP CSP. This means parentheses are evaluated first, then multiplication, division, and MOD from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. MOD has the SAME precedence as * and / — this is specifically stated in the CED and frequently tested.

rows: Left to right when at the same level
Left to right when at the same level

content.code:
-- Order of operations examples:

x ← 2 + 3 * 4
-- Step 1: * before + → 3*4 = 12
-- Step 2: 2 + 12 = 14
-- x = 14 (NOT 20)

y ← 10 MOD 3 + 2
-- Step 1: MOD before + → 10 MOD 3 = 1
-- Step 2: 1 + 2 = 3
-- y = 3

z ← 10 MOD 3 * 2
-- MOD and * have EQUAL precedence → left to right
-- Step 1: 10 MOD 3 = 1
-- Step 2: 1 * 2 = 2
-- z = 2

a ← (2 + 3) * 4
-- Step 1: parentheses first → 2+3 = 5
-- Step 2: 5 * 4 = 20
-- a = 20

b ← 8 + 4 / 2 - 1
-- Step 1: / before + and - → 4/2 = 2
-- Step 2: left to right → 8+2 = 10
-- Step 3: 10-1 = 9
-- b = 9

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: MOD has the SAME precedence as * and / — not lower. When you see MOD alongside * or / in the same expression without parentheses, evaluate left to right. This is directly tested on the exam. Also: always fully evaluate the right side before assigning — sequential statements execute in the order they appear.
Tracing Sequences of Mathematical Expressions

Sequential statements execute in the order they appear in the code segment. When tracing a sequence of assignment statements with mathematical expressions, evaluate each line in order, updating variable values as you go.
